Mortification
mor-tih-fih-KAY-shun
noun (the putting to death of sin)
From the Latin mortificatio, a putting to death, from mors (death) and facere (to make); the Spirit-wrought slaying of indwelling sin in the believer.

See also: Mortification · Mortification

📖 Biblical Definition

Mortification is the believer's lifelong work, wrought by the Holy Spirit, of putting to death the deeds of the body and the remaining corruption of indwelling sin. The apostle commands it directly: “If ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live,” and “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry.” It rests upon a finished fact—the old man is crucified with Christ, and they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts—and it issues in a continual duty: the believer must daily slay what Christ has already condemned. John Owen's famous maxim states the doctrine's urgency: “Be killing sin, or it will be killing you.” Mortification is not the eradication of sin in this life, for the flesh lusts against the Spirit to the end; nor is it mere outward restraint, the cutting off of acts while the root is cherished; it is the weakening, starving, and slaying of sin at its root by the power of the indwelling Spirit, through faith in Christ, by the means of grace. The dictionary marks the doctrine against two errors: the perfectionism that claims sin can be wholly rooted out now, and the therapeutic spirit that reframes sin as mere brokenness to be managed and healed rather than mortified. The believer does not negotiate with his sin or merely cope with it; by the Spirit he puts it to death, the negative side of that sanctification whose positive side is the quickening of the new man unto holiness.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Spirit-wrought putting to death of indwelling sin in the believer (Romans 8:13; Colossians 3:5), resting on the old man's crucifixion with Christ; not eradication nor mere restraint, but the daily slaying of sin at the root.

expand to see more

MORTIFICATION, noun. [Latin mors, death, and facere, to make.] The putting to death of indwelling sin by the Spirit.

“If ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live” (Romans 8:13).

It rests on a finished fact: the old man is crucified with Christ (Romans 6:6).

It is not eradication of sin in this life, nor mere outward restraint, but the slaying of sin at its root.

Owen: “Be killing sin, or it will be killing you.”

📖 Key Scripture

Ro 8:13 — "For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live."

Col 3:5 — "Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry:"

Ga 5:24 — "And they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts."

Ro 6:6 — "Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Perfectionism claims sin can be wholly eradicated now, while the therapeutic spirit reframes sin as brokenness to be managed and healed rather than put to death.

expand to see more

Perfectionism, in its Wesleyan and Keswick and modern revivalist forms, teaches that the believer may reach a state in which indwelling sin is eradicated or rendered inactive, often by a single crisis of consecration. The dictionary rejects this. Scripture commands ongoing mortification precisely because sin remains: the flesh lusts against the Spirit to the end of life, and the apostle who said the old man was crucified still commanded daily slaying of its deeds. To claim sin gone is to deceive oneself; the duty of mortification is lifelong because the warfare is lifelong.

The more fashionable corruption is the therapeutic, which relabels sin as “brokenness,” “woundedness,” or “unhealthy patterns” to be managed, processed, and healed, rather than confessed and mortified. This empties the doctrine of its moral seriousness and its hope. Scripture does not call the believer to manage his lusts but to kill them, not to cope with sin but to crucify it, by the power of the indwelling Spirit. The dictionary recovers mortification as real spiritual warfare: sin is an enemy to be slain, not a condition to be soothed, and the Spirit gives the believer both the duty and the strength to put it to death.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Latin mors (death) and facere (to make); the Greek thanatoo (to put to death) and nekroo (to mortify) name the slaying of the deeds of the body.

expand to see more

Mors, Latin, death; mortificare, to put to death, the root of “mortify.”

Thanatoo, Greek, to put to death, in Romans 8:13.

Nekroo, Greek, to make dead or mortify, in Colossians 3:5.

Stauroo, Greek, to crucify, of the flesh crucified with its affections (Galatians 5:24).

The “old man” (Greek palaios anthropos) is the unregenerate self crucified with Christ.

Usage

"The pastor pressed Owen's maxim, that the believer must be killing sin daily or sin will be killing him."

"He warned against the therapy that manages sin instead of mortifying it by the Spirit."

"She set herself, in the strength of the indwelling Spirit, to starve and slay the lust she once cherished."
